title: Aid cuts, expertise and the choices ahead
label: 17 November 2026 · FCDO spending and reform
summary: Senior Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office officials were questioned about staff cuts, shrinking aid budgets and a greater reliance on international organisations. They argued that predictable budgets, specialist advice and larger partners can help the UK achieve more with less money, but acknowledged gaps in staffing, harm from some country-level cuts and shortcomings in public reporting. Members pressed them for clearer evidence of results and better plans for countries losing support.

chapters.title: A smaller department in a harder world
chapters.takeaway: Officials said reduced aid and staff numbers require different choices, while members questioned whether valuable experience is being lost.

turns.speaker: Lindy Cameron
turns.text: I’ve just become the FCDO’s senior official. Nick and I will share the work: I’m likely to focus more on the department’s overall direction and operations, while he continues to oversee its aid and other programmes.

evidence.quote: Effectively, we are going to share the job between us. I am sure it will change over time, but essentially, as I work my way into the role, I will probably take more interest in some of the corporate and strategic issues; Nick will continue to be the accounting officer for the ODA and non-ODA programme.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: The Home Office also spends a large share of UK aid. Tim, do you oversee that spending as well?

evidence.quote: Now, a very large chunk is still in the Home Office. Do you have oversight of how all ODA is spent, or just that within the FCDO now?

turns.speaker: Tim Jones
turns.text: No. As finance director, I’m responsible for money that goes through the FCDO’s budget, not other departments’ spending.

evidence.quote: As the FCDO’s finance director, I am responsible for that which flows through our parliamentary estimates, rather than that of other Departments.
Yes, that is my remit.

turns.speaker: Tracy Gilbert
turns.text: What’s the biggest challenge for the UK’s development work?

evidence.quote: Lindy, what do you see as the biggest challenges facing the FCDO’s development agenda?

turns.speaker: Lindy Cameron
turns.text: The world is more conflict-ridden, countries want different things from us, and we have less aid money. I don’t think development needs another urgent reorganisation. I want staff with development expertise to feel valued and to see a future in the department.

evidence.quote: The biggest challenge is simply that the world is more contested, more complicated and more conflict-ridden than it was when I was last in the Department.
what has changed is that what countries want from us has changed.
reduced aid obviously affects what we do.
on the development side I think a lot of change has just happened, so I do not think urgent changes are needed now.
development professionals within the organisation feel valued for their skills and expertise, can see their career paths as part of a future in the Department

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Staff cuts began before you arrived. I’m concerned they went ahead before the department properly checked which skills it had, and that experienced people are leaving. Will you change course?

evidence.quote: It was not until more than a year later that there was actually an audit of the skills that you had.
Are you planning to continue it in its current form, or are there aspects that you are looking to revisit, pause or change?
My concern all the way through this has been that gap

turns.speaker: Lindy Cameron
turns.text: The department had become unusually senior-heavy, limiting opportunities for junior staff. But I agree we must protect expertise. I’ve asked for a review of people who still have no permanent role, to check which important skills we could lose in the final phase.

evidence.quote: It had become quite top-heavy, so we had a lot of SCS and grade 6 staff. There were many brilliant experts, but it was nevertheless crowding out some of our brilliant junior staff.
I have asked for a review of who we have in the redeployment pool, to make sure we understand what key skills we could lose in that last phase

turns.speaker: Nick Dyer
turns.text: We’ve lost experience, and my biggest worry is unfilled specialist jobs. About 14% of our advisory posts are vacant, especially in statistics, economics, climate and health. Recruitment restrictions held us back; now we need to hire, as well as consider training people already here.

evidence.quote: I think we have lost quite a bit of experience.
About 14% of our posts are still unfilled, and that is concentrated in four main areas: our statistics advisers, economists, climate people and health people.
we put a block on recruitment because of our affordability gap. Frankly, we have not recruited enough people and now we need to get on and recruit.
We have accredited some people internally, who have come into the advisory cadres.

turns.speaker: Brian Mathew
turns.text: How many engineers have you lost, and does the department still have the engineering expertise it needs?

evidence.quote: Could you give us an idea of how many qualified civil, mechanical, roads and water engineers you have lost? What engineering capacity does FCDO have left, and is that a worry?

turns.speaker: Nick Dyer
turns.text: I’ll have to write with the engineering figures. The broader group covering livelihoods, climate and infrastructure has fallen from 135 to 101 advisers in 18 months, but I can’t say how many of those were infrastructure specialists.

evidence.quote: I would have to write to you on that; I just do not have the numbers.
That cadre has gone down from 135 to 101, so that is 34 people over the last 18 months. I would have to dig into that and have a look at what the actual infrastructure component of that is

turns.speaker: Lindy Cameron
turns.text: The restructuring is close to finishing, but I won’t set a date. At the start of this week, 220 staff had no permanent job while 588 jobs were being advertised. We need to handle that carefully for the people affected.

evidence.quote: We are close but not there yet. As of the beginning of this week, I think there were 220 staff in the redeployment pool without a substantive job, but we had 588 roles under recruitment.
I do not have a date, and I would not want to put a date on when we, in a sense, bring this to an end.
The most important people at this phase are the ones who do not have a job and want to know what is happening to them next.

chapters.title: Who provides expert advice?
chapters.takeaway: Country offices are changing their teams as budgets fall, but central groups of experts are not intended to replace permanent specialists overseas.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: As country offices prepare for cuts, will they still have the specialists they need on the ground?

evidence.quote: My concern about that is whether you will have the people on the ground—literally—who you need.

turns.speaker: Nick Dyer
turns.text: We gave offices early budget figures so they could plan their teams. I’ve checked choices in Nigeria and Zimbabwe and found them sensible, but we’ll need to review the overall picture when this phase ends. Central expert groups cannot simply replace advisers a country office has let go.

evidence.quote: We deliberately gave the country offices early indications of what their allocations would be in early 2025-26, exactly so they could start thinking about what shape they needed to be and what skills they needed to deliver on that bilateral allocation.
I have done a deep dive on Nigeria and Zimbabwe, and the choices that they made were quite sensible.
That is not what the communities of expertise are for; they are for something else.
Once this phase is over, we need to take stock and ask ourselves whether the shape overseas still looks and feels right.

turns.speaker: Monica Harding
turns.text: So what are these central groups actually meant to provide?

evidence.quote: When you referred to reliance on the communities of expertise and having that kind of resource hub, was that about capacity or capability shortages in post?

turns.speaker: Nick Dyer
turns.text: There are nine groups intended to connect country offices with specialist knowledge, including experts outside government. They can advise on what works and fund short visits or some longer support. But if an office needs a health adviser for six months, it should employ one.

evidence.quote: We have created nine of these communities of expertise.

The purpose of them, first, is to provide a sort of helpdesk function where you can come and identify, talk about and get advice on what is working and what is not working and how to access this world-class capability.
They also provide some modest money to provide and fund short-term three-month technical inputs into a country visit on a particular issue of interest or, in some cases, longer-term support
If you need a health adviser, you should employ one.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: The groups’ purpose has changed as they’ve been set up. If the education group still runs programmes from London, isn’t that at odds with giving countries more control?

evidence.quote: Then, I think it was centre of expertise, then it became community of expertise, then it looked like it was really going to be in charge of the centrally managed funds programme and then it was not.
There was meant to be a shift to the countries making the decisions on where their money was going, but really, you have just created another body to keep the money in London.

turns.speaker: Nick Dyer
turns.text: We’re ending many programmes previously run from the centre, but some existing ones still need managing. The education group also shares evidence and has advised Malawi and Ethiopia on teaching. You’re right that the groups have caused confusion; some are established, while others will take another year or two.

evidence.quote: We are deliberately exiting quite a lot of centrally managed programmes, because we think that those have run their course
we still have some legacy centrally managed programmes that need some management, so they are going into the communities of expertise.
The education team have also provided technical advice to, I think, Malawi and Ethiopia on how to improve the curriculum or teacher training
there has been some confusion on this, both externally and internally
some of them are well established and some are going to take another year or two to set up.

chapters.title: Preparing for disasters with less aid
chapters.takeaway: Officials defended a smaller emergency reserve and Nepal’s planned aid cut by pointing to early warnings and faster access to prearranged funding.

turns.speaker: Monica Harding
turns.text: With aid being cut, is there enough left in the emergency fund for unexpected disasters?

evidence.quote: How much of the crisis fund has been allocated so far for 2026-27? Is the remaining funding sufficient to respond to unforeseen crises, given the cuts to ODA?

turns.speaker: Nick Dyer
turns.text: We’ve allocated £37.4 million of this year’s £75 million fund. Based on past sudden disasters, I think £75 million is enough for that purpose. Separately, we’ve allocated about £1.4 billion a year for humanitarian work, including longer-running crises.

evidence.quote: Of the £75 million that we allocated for 2026-27, we have currently allocated £37.4 million.
we have generally funded those responses to between £30 million and £50 million a year, so the £75 million is sufficient for that sudden-onset experience.
on top of that we have allocated about £1.4 billion a year for our humanitarian response over the course of the next SR.

turns.speaker: Monica Harding
turns.text: Nepal’s UK aid allocation is expected to fall by 89% over three years. Are you reconsidering that after the recent floods?

evidence.quote: Nepal’s ODA allocation is expected to fall by 89% over the next three years. Are you considering revising those plans, given the flooding that happened recently?

turns.speaker: Nick Dyer
turns.text: Ministers haven’t signalled a change. With the UK money available, we’re helping Nepal improve flood warnings and arrange finance that can pay out quickly when disaster strikes. That can get money to the country sooner than waiting for donors to make grants afterward.

evidence.quote: Ministers we have spoken to are keen to ensure that we have predictability in our allocations, and they are not signalling yet that we should be revising them.
One is to invest in Nepal’s early warning mechanisms.
The second is to help Nepal develop its prearranged finance mechanism, so that if, sadly, a flood or an earthquake hits Nepal, additional money will be made available very quickly.
quite often we rely on donors to provide grants a long time after the event has happened

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: If Nepal’s disaster risks are predictable, is a much smaller UK allocation really realistic?

evidence.quote: So if it is predictable that it is likely to have crises like this and they are going to be exacerbated by climate change, Ministers believe that predicting that they are going to get £5 million a year from 2028-29 is better than having something that is realistic in place that deals with the level of threat that that country is under.

turns.speaker: Nick Dyer
turns.text: I’m not saying the UK’s own programme must cover the whole risk. We can help Nepal build systems to respond, and use our influence with organisations such as the World Bank to support that work.

evidence.quote: I don’t think we are saying that.
we need to create the institutions and mechanisms in Nepal that allow Nepal itself to be able to manage and respond to the crises that hit it
I do not think we need to do it ourselves through our bilateral programme, but we can use our expertise and relationships to help Nepal build it themselves.

turns.speaker: Tulip Siddiq
turns.text: What about preventing damage in the first place—for example, through where and how homes are built?

evidence.quote: Is there a preventive angle to this as well? I am not naive; I know you cannot actually stop a flood. I am thinking of the way houses are built and the town planning and things like that.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: I mean beyond Nepal too. Are you considering future climate risks whenever the UK advises on or invests in buildings and other infrastructure?

evidence.quote: I am not talking about Nepal specifically. Nepal needs to be the wake-up call.
Are we doing the same thing around the world, knowing the climate change that is happening?
Maybe it should be a line in all our negotiations that it is a consideration.

turns.speaker: Nick Dyer
turns.text: We have examples, including buildings designed for floods in Bangladesh and planning for hotter cities. Climate adaptation work is intended to address such risks. But I can’t say we consider them everywhere, every time.

evidence.quote: We do urban planning that takes into account how cities are becoming hotter, and how you can respond to that. In Bangladesh, we are providing support to look at structures, such as increasing the height of houses in flood-prone areas.
Can I say in front of you that we are doing that absolutely everywhere, every time we are doing some climate work? I am not sure that I could quite make that commitment
All our adaptation work is about how you adapt to a changing climate

turns.speaker: Nick Dyer
turns.text: On climate funding for nature, we expect broadly a quarter to go to nature, but won’t make that a binding target. Past targets have pushed spending choices in the wrong direction. Instead, we’ve promised more regular reports on spending and results.

evidence.quote: if you put hard targets into your funding, it actually distorts the choices that you are making.
we expect that broadly about 25% of the funding will go to nature, but we are not setting those as hard targets.
we commit in our response to being a lot more transparent and regular about our funding and also the results that we are achieving.

chapters.title: Where aid goes—and what the public can see
chapters.takeaway: Members challenged whether larger international organisations make up for direct UK aid cuts and whether the department explains the results clearly enough.

turns.speaker: Dr Rushworth
turns.text: Does putting more aid through international organisations deliver more than funding countries directly?

evidence.quote: I want to ask about the shift to multilateral funding at the expense of bilateral funding. Lindy, does spending through multilaterals achieve more impact?

turns.speaker: Nick Dyer
turns.text: They can work at a scale we can’t achieve alone. For every pound the UK puts into the World Bank’s IDA fund, it brings in another £3. Organisations buying vaccines in bulk can also lower prices. But we expect the organisations we fund to improve how they work.

evidence.quote: For every pound we put into IDA, they leverage an additional £3 to put into their relationships and their investments in countries.
With the Global Fund and Gavi, the fact that you are doing bulk procurement drives down prices
We will fund you, but we want to see the humanitarian system reform

turns.speaker: Lindy Cameron
turns.text: It shouldn’t be an either-or choice. Staff working directly in countries can see what international organisations are doing and challenge them. That helps the UK make better decisions when it funds those organisations.

evidence.quote: I do not think it is either/or. Making the two work in tandem has always been a strength of ours in development.
Our brilliant expertise on the ground helps to inform the multilateral choices we make
I have seen some of our bilaterally funded staff go toe-to-toe with multilaterals on what they are doing.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: But when was the last time you reviewed whether those organisations deliver value? And how can an ordinary taxpayer see what UK money achieves through them?

evidence.quote: I think the last review of the value of multilaterals was in 2016. With all the changes that you have detailed, is it now time to do a review to see if they do deliver?
could it do any job of communicating where our money goes?

turns.speaker: Nick Dyer
turns.text: The organisations publish extensive project and results information, though I take the point that people won’t search a World Bank database. For example, our £1.25 billion investment in Gavi is expected to immunise 109 million children and save 1.95 million lives. We need to tell that story better.

evidence.quote: The World Bank has a corporate scorecard that it reports every year against the outputs and outcomes that it is actually delivering.
I could point you to the World Bank database on its projects and programmes.
Our £1.25 billion investment in Gavi is going to immunise 109 million children and save 1.95 million lives. We need to tell that story better.

turns.speaker: Dr Rushworth
turns.text: Even if total aid to Africa holds up through international organisations, what happens in individual countries when UK-funded services lose support? Sudan’s education budget is one example.

evidence.quote: We heard evidence in this Committee from Sudan, for example, where 90% of its education budget was UK supported and that has been withdrawn.

although the overall package to Africa as a continent might have increased, we are seeing examples of particular countries that are naming the UK as a donor that pulled the rug out from under them quite rapidly.

turns.speaker: Nick Dyer
turns.text: These are real choices: more money for international health and humanitarian organisations leaves less for bilateral aid. We published an assessment acknowledging that the cuts would have effects. Ministers protected some funding for women, girls and education, and directed a greater share of direct country aid toward fragile countries.

evidence.quote: The more we put in those parts of the multilateral system, the less we have to spend on the bilaterals. That is basically the trade-off.
we are also clear in the equality impact assessment that we did and that we published that there will be some impacts in terms of the reduction in the bilateral programmes
There was a decision to relatively protect and in some cases to fully protect our funding to women and girls, and to education.
The share of our bilateral programme going into fragile countries has gone up from 57% to 71%

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: In Sierra Leone, UK support helped cut maternal deaths, but its health funding has now dropped sharply. Nurses and medicines need paying for. Are you actually helping the country manage that change, rather than assuming someone else will step in?

evidence.quote: We have done a fantastic job; we have cut maternal mortality by 80%.

Last year, however, we cut the funding for their health from £35 million to just under £1 million now—I think that’s right—and there was no “glide path”; we have just cut the funding, so they cannot pay nurses and they cannot buy drugs.
You can, or you are doing?

turns.speaker: Nick Dyer
turns.text: Teams should look for other funders, help governments organise services and work with international partners. But I can’t say what the Sierra Leone team is doing specifically. We can’t prevent every harmful effect of these cuts.

evidence.quote: We cannot pretend that this is not difficult, we cannot pretend it will not have impacts, and we cannot mitigate all the impacts in all the cases.

What we can do is try to find alternative sources for the funding. We can help Governments to themselves try to work out institutionally how better to organise and buy things, such as drugs; and we can work with our multilateral partners
I am not on the ground in Sierra Leone, but I would be surprised if our teams in-country are not doing that.

turns.speaker: Dr Rushworth
turns.text: Can smaller local organisations still get UK funding? They may be able to make a pound go further in their communities than a large organisation can.

evidence.quote: UK aid, when it was spent through country offices, was often based on relationships between FCDO staff—or DFID staff, as they once were—and civil society organisations working locally at grassroots, where they could stretch a tax pound much further
But the third parties used to be smaller and more local, where decision making is more local because the relationships were there?

turns.speaker: Nick Dyer
turns.text: Some programmes do work through local partners, but people tell us our application requirements are too difficult. We’re trying to simplify them so smaller organisations can seek funding. Doing that properly while checking how money is used is substantial work.

evidence.quote: We have examples of country programmes that are trying to do more local delivery through local partners. What most people tell us is that we are too bureaucratic and too difficult to work with as an organisation.
We are simplifying and trying to strip back some of the expectations of our partners, so that some smaller partners can apply for our funding.
Yes, we are, but it is a really heavy lift to do this and do it properly.

chapters.title: Reporting results and setting priorities
chapters.takeaway: The department promised better project information, but ministers do not plan to publish a single new development strategy.

turns.speaker: Dr Rushworth
turns.text: The UK has received its lowest score yet in an international ranking of aid transparency. What went wrong?

evidence.quote: The UK received its lowest score in this year’s aid transparency index since it began in 2011. What does the FCDO need to do to be more transparent?

turns.speaker: Nick Dyer
turns.text: Three things hurt the score: we published country budgets late, information is available for only about 83% of our projects, and there’s no new document called a development strategy. We’ve published the budgets and plan a new project-information website next year. Ministers don’t expect to publish a separate strategy.

evidence.quote: One is that we had not set out our allocations by country.
the number of our projects that we publish data on has dropped to about 83%. The last is that we have not set out a strategy for development.
We have fixed the first, and I think we have fixed the second as well—next year, we will launch a new DevTracker
Our Ministers are not expecting to set out a new development strategy

turns.speaker: James Naish
turns.text: If ministers change, wouldn’t a written strategy help staff and the public understand which priorities endure? Other countries are publishing theirs.

evidence.quote: are other countries renewing and publishing strategies in a way that we as the UK are not? Will a gap be left by us choosing not to republish?
We are already on our third Minister in two and a half years.
not having foundational documents that outline the strategy for our approach to international development is a good thing. It only adds to the uncertainty and challenges we face.

turns.speaker: Lindy Cameron
turns.text: Ministers have explained their development approach in speeches, even if it isn’t in one document titled ‘development strategy’. But I agree we need to think about the department’s lasting purpose after the merger, and improve planning for our overseas offices.

evidence.quote: we are not publishing something entitled “development strategy”, but Ministers have laid out clearly what their approach to development is.
post-merger, there is something about the enduring purpose of the organisation and the way everyone sees themselves in it. That is a live conversation
Something I take very seriously is that it is important that we run the network of overseas offices for the whole of Government.
We brought in place last year for the first time a new country business plan process.

turns.speaker: Brian Mathew
turns.text: Can you show whether the government’s commitment to women and girls is changing outcomes? And what information do you collect about people with disabilities?

evidence.quote: What data does the FCDO capture on how its projects help women and girls, and is that data enough to effectively hold the Minister to account?
How would you assess the FCDO’s capturing and use of data on the impact of ODA spending on people with disabilities?

turns.speaker: Nick Dyer
turns.text: We can track funding and projects aimed at women and girls, including support for mothers. Where possible, we also break down results by gender, disability, age and location. That isn’t a complete picture of every group or every outcome.

evidence.quote: we can track that 90% in terms of the funding.
we can track how many mothers are supported and how many lives are saved through that.
where we disaggregate, where possible we focus on four things: gender, disability, age and geography.
That misses quite a lot of other protected characteristics.

chapters.title: Investment, debt and financial risk
chapters.takeaway: Officials said investment and loan guarantees can bring in money beyond the aid budget, but acknowledged limits on what the department can fund or safely promise.

turns.speaker: Tulip Siddiq
turns.text: If the UK wants to invest rather than only give grants, why is funding for British International Investment being reduced?

evidence.quote: How does the reduced funding for BII fit with the FCDO’s shift from a donor to an investor model?

turns.speaker: Nick Dyer
turns.text: BII remains part of that approach, but the Treasury has given us much less money of the kind used to add to its investment funds. BII now needs to remain financially sustainable without further large payments from us. The shift toward investment also includes working through the World Bank.

evidence.quote: BII is clearly part of our investment offer.
the type of capital that we are given by the Treasury to do things such as invest in BII has come down quite significantly. We are no longer able to capitalise its balance sheet.
The donor to investment model is as much about what we are doing through the likes of the World Bank
the challenge for BII now is how it ensures financial sustainability without additional funding from the FCDO.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: BII’s investments are large. How do you make sure its decisions really meet your goals for poorer countries, climate and women, rather than just sound good in presentations?

evidence.quote: I think that as the bilateral and multilateral budget is shrinking for FCDO, BII needs to sweat a little bit more for your policies, and it is whether you have the influence and oversight to be able to do that.
are you sure that, for example, their definition of climate is the same as the one that you are working to?

turns.speaker: Nick Dyer
turns.text: We meet BII regularly and have set expectations for its next five years: 25% of new investments in the least developed countries, 45% on climate and 30% benefiting women. I’m fairly sure its definitions match ours, but I’ll check. We shouldn’t have civil servants making its individual business investments.

evidence.quote: we have quarterly shareholder meetings with BII and monthly meetings with the CEO and members of the board
We expect it to spend 25% of its new investments in the least developed countries, 45% on climate and 30% on benefiting women in employment and investors.
I will go away and check with my team, but I am pretty sure that that is the case.
we should leave that to the professionals

turns.speaker: James Naish
turns.text: Where does debt relief fit in? What’s different from the big debt-relief effort around 2000?

evidence.quote: How is the FCDO planning to retain both expertise and resources in that particular area? And where do debt relief and debt sustainability sit in the FCDO’s overarching objectives?
If you compare this to HIPC of the Jubilee debt in 2000, I would say that two things are different.

turns.speaker: Nick Dyer
turns.text: Many countries now owe more to private lenders and China. For some, the immediate problem isn’t the total debt but costly repayments that leave too little for health and education. We’re examining whether expensive, short-term debts can be replaced with cheaper loans repaid over longer periods. Better records of who owes what are essential.

evidence.quote: you now have a lot more private creditors and you have a lot of Chinese debt
The size of the debt is not a problem, but it is the payment they have got to make on it—the interest rates they are being charged on the debt
they are basically spending more on debt service than they are on health and education in many cases
how can you refinance debt that is high-cost and short-maturity into longer-maturity and lower-cost debt?
You really have to understand that creditor data set.

turns.speaker: Dr Rushworth
turns.text: Campaigners say some private lenders obstruct debt relief and want UK law changed. Why isn’t the government doing that?

evidence.quote: Various groups, including as CAFOD and Christian Aid, have been campaigning for this. Do you know why the Government are resisting their demands?
a few bad lenders that are not willing to restructure some of that debt multilaterally.

turns.speaker: Nick Dyer
turns.text: We hear the campaigners, but in the debt restructurings we’ve observed, private lenders have played their part. If there’s evidence of holdouts, we’re open to it. So far, we haven’t seen a problem that requires legislation.

evidence.quote: Our observed experience is that they are. We hear what the NGOs are saying about bringing forward UK legislation to force creditors to play their part, but we have not observed a problem.
If there are, we are happy to be corrected, but we do not actually see a problem that needs to be fixed through legislation.

turns.speaker: James Naish
turns.text: What can you tell about the results when the UK gives a financial guarantee for a World Bank loan? And is there a limit to how much risk you’ll take?

evidence.quote: What information is the World Bank providing to the FCDO about the impact of loans that are supported by UK financial guarantees?
Is there a point when we say we are not going to do that any more because we are too exposed?

turns.speaker: Nick Dyer
turns.text: We normally link a guarantee to a known loan and can track what it funds. In Ukraine, for example, guaranteed World Bank lending has paid teachers’ salaries and pensions. We set limits on annual risk and on exposure to any one country, but deliberately exceeded both for Ukraine. That leaves very little room for more guarantees.

evidence.quote: we have £3.8 billion of existing guarantees to Ukraine through the World Bank, and we know that we have funded the salaries of 450,000 teachers
Ditto we provided pensions for 10 million pensioners in Ukraine
We set a limit on that annual risk
We have a limit that we attach to the annual exposure, and then there is a concentration risk as well.
Actually, we have broken both those limits because of Ukraine.
our guarantee headroom has pretty much disappeared.

chapters.title: What the budget allows
chapters.takeaway: Officials valued a predictable multi-year budget despite deep cuts, and said future aid targets would be addressed at the next spending review.

turns.speaker: Monica Harding
turns.text: If the Home Office spends less UK aid on supporting refugees here than expected, could that money instead fund aid overseas?

evidence.quote: Have you had any discussions with the Treasury about whether that money will be reallocated into ODA spent overseas?

turns.speaker: Nick Dyer
turns.text: We’ve had no indication of an underspend this year. Under the agreement made at the spending review, the Home Office keeps any underspend and must cover any overspend. Our official expectation is that the money wouldn’t come to the FCDO, though ministers could discuss it politically.

evidence.quote: No, we have not had an indication that they will underspend this year.
If the Home Office overspends, it has to find the money; if it underspends, it will absorb the money.
That is a political conversation. In terms of the official-level agreement at the SR and our official-level expectations now, that funding would not come to us.

turns.speaker: Brian Mathew
turns.text: If UK aid is meant to reach 0.3% of national income, shouldn’t the department press for more money if the figures show it’s falling short?

evidence.quote: Given that it is estimated that FCDO has effectively been short-changed to the tune of around £320 million on the 0.3% commitment, what can you do and what will you be doing
given that the amount is expected to grow, surely you as a Department, and us as your scrutineers, should be keeping an eye on this.

turns.speaker: Tim Jones
turns.text: Our budget was agreed for several years rather than adjusted whenever national income changes. That gives teams certainty after years of sudden increases and cuts. We expect to discuss how much is needed to meet the target in the next spending review, not adjust the budget each year.

evidence.quote: the spending review period we are in was negotiated on the understanding that we would have a very settled, predictable budget that would run for a multi-year period.
it does not get adjusted as we go, tracking GNI movements.
We fully anticipate that this will be a live part of our conversations with the Treasury on the next spending review

turns.speaker: James Naish
turns.text: With spending falling, can you still pay for frontline programmes and the staff needed overseas?

evidence.quote: given that fall and trajectory, how confident are you that the frontline programmes, staffing and requirements of the overseas network can still be delivered with that level of reduction to day-to-day spending?

turns.speaker: Tim Jones
turns.text: We agreed to bring the department’s running costs back to the same cash level at the end of this spending review as at the start. The £290 million transformation funding is intended to help lower ongoing costs. We also have more freedom to hire staff rather than outsource some work, if that gives taxpayers better value.

evidence.quote: we agreed to be at the same cash level at the end of this spending review period as we were at the start—that is the flat cash—but that the £290 million of transformation funding that I referenced at the start would be our investment to reduce the cost base
in certain types of development programming, and in things like digital, it is massively to the taxpayers’ benefit to create civil servant roles rather than to outsource it.

turns.speaker: Lindy Cameron
turns.text: That flexibility matters, especially for digital skills. The restructuring has been painful, but its aim is to lower staff costs enough that we can make real choices in future about investing in people or technology.

evidence.quote: The area where we will use it most, if I am honest, is in the digital skills.

the transformation funding allowed us to do restructuring that has been painful, but none the less allowed us to bring down the run rate of our staff costs to a level at which we then have more flexibility to decide whether we are investing in people or technology
